seo.title: Plugin Hosting Groupings {'|'} plugin-hostd {'|'} OpenMixer
seo.description: How plugin-hostd and the other hosts pack the same plugins into programs, what each arrangement trades, and what the benchmark measures for each.

hero.title: Plugin Hosting Groupings
hero.lede: When the console runs effects and instruments, the same plugins can be packed into programs in different ways. Each way trades CPU and memory against safety: how much else a crashing plugin takes down with it. The benchmark measures each way side by side. This page explains the words and draws every arrangement.

words.title: Six things nest inside each other
words.intro: Every arrangement below is built from the same pieces, always nested in the same order. The colours stay the same in every drawing on this page.

jack.name: JACK graph
jack.body: The audio engine that moves sound between programs, one block of samples at a time, at one sample rate (48000, 96000…) and one block size, the quantum (64, 128, 256, 512 frames).
jack.eg: Each program in the graph is a JACK client with its own ports. Every block, JACK wakes each client in order; a client that is late causes an xrun, an audible click.

plugin.name: Plugin
plugin.body: One effect or instrument: a compressor, a delay, a synth. It is a library (CLAP or LV2), not a program: it only runs inside a host.
plugin.eg: CLAP and LV2 are the two plugin formats. Some plugins ship in both.

proc.name: Process
proc.body: A running program with its own memory. If a plugin inside it crashes, the whole process dies, along with every other plugin in it.
proc.eg: More processes: more isolation, more memory, more switching between them every block.

worker.name: Worker
worker.body: A process that plugin-hostd starts to run plugins. plugin-hostd itself (the daemon) only takes commands; the sound runs in its workers.
worker.eg: The daemon decides how many workers there are and which plugins each one holds.

chain.name: Chain
chain.body: Plugins joined in series inside one worker: the output of one feeds the next directly, in memory, without going back out through JACK between them.
chain.eg: Cheapest way to run several plugins; one crash stops the whole chain.

pool.name: Pool
pool.body: One shared worker that takes in the plugins that are allowed to share, wherever they sit in the signal path, so they do not each need a worker of their own.
pool.eg: Plugins marked "isolated" never enter a pool.

words.more: Two more words matter. A host is the program that loads plugins: four are compared (below). A pin is the qualification verdict stored for each plugin: in-process means it may share a process, isolated means it must run alone because it misbehaved when measured (it crashed, hung, or broke real-time rules).

h1.what: OpenMixer's own host: one process holding many plugins.
h1.formats: CLAP, and LV2 through its adapter

h2.what: OpenMixer's supervisor: a daemon that runs plugins in workers and can group them (chains, plans, pools). Its workers are omx-clap-host processes.

h3.what: The reference host from the MOD project: one process holding many plugins.

h4.what: The reference minimal host: one process per plugin, always.

fig.poolGraphNote: on grp8: 5 workers with the pool, 7 with the plan, 8 one per plugin
fig.poolFlow: The signal still flows comp → drive → delay → drive → comp through JACK; the pool only changes which worker holds each plugin.

modes.title: Six ways to run the same plugins
modes.intro: Each drawing runs the same three plugins, A → B → C, between a test signal (a sine wave, or chords for instruments) and the output.

individual.title: Individual
individual.body: Every plugin gets a process of its own. Sound goes out through JACK and back in between each plugin.
individual.tradeoff: Safest, and the most expensive: three programs in memory, and JACK switches between three processes every block.

shared.title: Shared process
shared.body: One host program holds every plugin and connects them itself.

tally.b: JACK clients 3 (one per plugin, linked through JACK)

shared.tradeoff: Cheapest in memory. Each plugin is still a JACK client of its own inside the host, so sound goes through JACK between them. A single faulty plugin takes the whole host down.

chain.title: Chain
chain.body: plugin-hostd first adds each plugin, then moves them all into one worker as a chain. The daemon stays outside the sound path and only gives orders.

tally.b: JACK clients 1 (omx-clap-host runs a CLAP chain as one client)
tally.c: a crash stops the chain; the culprit is quarantined and the rest go on

chain.tradeoff: The sound passes from plugin to plugin in memory when the worker runs the chain as one JACK client (omx-clap-host); a mod-host worker keeps one client per plugin.

chainAdd.title: Chain, added in place
chainAdd.body: The same result as a chain, built differently: each plugin is added straight into the chain's worker and never gets a worker of its own first. This row measures what it costs to build the chain, not only to run it.

plan.title: Plan
plan.body: plugin-hostd's planner reads every plugin's pin, its cost and its running history. A run of two or more neighbours that may share becomes a chain (chain:1.<k>); a plugin pinned isolated gets a worker of its own and cuts the strip there. With grouping off, the default, the plan is only answered and nothing moves. The bench's grouping test repeats comp, drive, delay, drive, comp, with every drive pinned isolated: on grp8 that comes to 7 segments, on grp16 to 13.
plan.small: With longer runs of shareable plugins, each segment between two isolated plugins holds several of them as a chain. The bench refuses a plan that comes back as one single segment, since that would just repeat the chain row.
plan.tradeoff: The isolation the pins ask for, and sharing everywhere else.
plan.more: How the planner chooses the segments: the grouping planner

pool.title: Pool

tags.a: H2 plugin-hostd · plan, then pool g1

pool.body: Start from the plan. Then every plugin the plan left in a worker of its own, but that its pin allows to share, moves into one shared pool worker. Isolated plugins stay alone.
pool.tradeoff: The fewest processes that still respect every pin.
pool.more: How pools are placed and reported: plugin-hostd placement

compare.title: Five rows, two test families
compare.intro: The benchmark compares five rows. Four hosts make five rows because omx-clap-host is measured on both of its formats, and plugin-hostd is measured both single and grouped.

jalv.scenarios: cvc and cvl (always the LV2 builds)

modhost.scenarios: cvc and cvl (always the LV2 builds)

hostd.arrangement:
single: individual
grouped: chain, chain added in place, plan, pool

chains.title: Chains vs processes
chains.eg: Rows: plugin-hostd individual, chain and chain added in place; omx-clap-host and mod-host shared; jalv individual. It asks: how much does grouping save, and how do the hosts compare on the same plugins?

grouping.title: Grouping vs processes
grouping.body: grp8 and grp16: 8 and 16 plugins (comp, drive, delay, drive, comp, repeated), every drive pinned isolated.
grouping.eg: Rows: plugin-hostd individual, chain, plan and pool. It asks: does the planner keep the isolation the pins ask for while costing close to a full chain?

measured.title: Each row, in numbers
measured.intro: The first four figures are the ones to compare first; the rest explain them.

dsp.meaning: How much of each audio block's time JACK spends processing. Higher means less room before clicks.

rss.meaning: Memory held by every process of the row together.

add.meaning: From the first add to the last reply: for the two chain rows until the chain runs, for jalv until the last client is in the graph. How long a user waits when building a strip.

xruns.meaning: Blocks that came too late: audible clicks during the measuring window.

latency.meaning: The delay from the source to the output, in frames, as JACK reports it at the output port: the sum of what every client on the path declares. Divide by the sample rate for milliseconds (256 frames at 48000 Hz is 5.3 ms). This is the declared path latency; plugin-qualify measures each plugin's real latency separately and keeps both in its records.

processes.meaning: How many programs the row runs, and how many of them appear in the JACK graph. This is where the arrangements differ most visibly.

pss.meaning: Memory of all the row's processes together: rss counts shared libraries in every process, pss splits them fairly between processes.

cpu.meaning: CPU time the row's processes used over the window, beside JACK's own DSP load.

ctx.meaning: How often the processes, and jackd itself, were switched out; involuntary switches are the ones that steal time from audio.

recover.meaning: In the kill test: how long plugin-hostd takes to put a worker back after it is killed.

level.meaning: The output is recorded for a second and its level checked, so a row that ran but produced silence never counts as a pass.

measured.runs: Every row runs twice: on a quiet machine, and beside a stress load (busy CPU cores and memory pressure), at each sample rate and block size. A row whose three repeats differ in DSP load by more than 10% (and more than 0.3 points) is run again once on its own, then marked unstable. A silent row is unstable too, and so is an output level more than 1 dB off the one-per-worker row.
measured.callout: The reference figures come from a private JACK server on the dummy driver with real-time priority, the same in a container on every machine. A run on a real audio interface (--alsa hw:X) is the hardware tier: it shows that interface's latency and xruns and is not compared with the reference.
measured.docs: The full page, with drawings, is in plugin-hostd's documentation: {link}.
